content: Events are promoted through social media platforms, typically attracting 10 to 20 male participants. Film screenings are often used as a starting point for discussions on community values and shared experiences. In addition to films, activities such as games and picnics are organized, alongside discussions on topics like healthy relationships, experiences with shame, and HIV prevention. These events serve as an invitation for young men to attend YouthCO workshops, which focus on education about HIV, safer sex practices, and sexual well-being. Young gay men are the primary organizers and leaders of all Mpowerment events, supported by YouthCO staff members who are under 30 years old. The project has successfully engaged hundreds of young gay men across British Columbia by empowering volunteers to take on leadership roles within their social networks. However, as the project relies on staff members to leverage their personal social networks, maintaining boundaries between personal and professional lives can be challenging. YouthCO emphasizes the importance of supporting staff in self-care to prevent burnout. Mpowerment has also recognized the value of creating accessible, youth-friendly community spaces where participants feel welcomed and accepted. These spaces provide free access to condoms and lubricants, further promoting sexual health and safety. The National AIDS Control Programme (NACP) in Afghanistan works at both national and local levels to increase community acceptance of harm reduction services for people who inject drugs. The program offers a comprehensive package of harm reduction and social services, operating a fixed facility in areas with high concentrations of drug users and deploying outreach teams to reach those hesitant to access formal services. Despite these efforts, stigma, discrimination, detention, and police violence remain significant barriers to service delivery. At the central level, NACP engages with law enforcement officials and ministry representatives to raise awareness about the challenges faced by people who inject drugs and the societal benefits of harm reduction. In the provinces, NACP conducts training and sensitization sessions for police officers, community elders, and religious leaders, involving service providers to foster collaboration between stakeholders and harm reduction services. To date, NACP has reached 8 out of 34 provinces and trained approximately 800 police officers. Anecdotal reports suggest improved understanding and acceptance of harm reduction services in areas where NACP activities have been implemented, with fewer instances of police harassment or violence. However, high turnover in police departments, particularly in the provinces, necessitates ongoing training for newly hired officers. In Nepal, recognizing the lack of specific laws and community-level services for people who inject drugs, Naya Goreto launched the Bridging the Gap: Health and Human Rights Programme for the Key Population. This initiative engages stakeholders ranging from parliamentarians to local councilors and public health officials in advocacy efforts addressing the needs of people who inject drugs. The program emphasizes the meaningful participation of drug users at all levels, training over 200 community members to lead activities such as situation analysis, advocacy campaigns, and program monitoring. A committee of key stakeholders has been established to advocate for the health and human rights of drug users, and community representatives are mobilized to participate in consultations with government officials. Advocacy efforts have led to the inclusion of drug-related issues in local government action plans and budgets for drug awareness programs. A member of the injecting drug user community now sits on the District AIDS Coordination Committee. In Portugal, legislative changes in 2001 decriminalized the possession of controlled drugs for personal use, redirecting individuals to dissuasion boards instead of prosecuting them. An independent study found that the number of drug users in treatment increased significantly, and new HIV cases among drug users decreased due to expanded harm reduction services. Contrary to concerns, there was no major increase in drug use; instead, reductions in problematic use, drug-related harms, and criminal justice system overcrowding were observed. Community organizations play a crucial role in reducing stigma and discrimination and improving access to services. For example, Agência Piaget para o Desenvolvimento in Portugal works with vulnerable populations, including drug users and sex workers, to promote harm reduction and reduce discrimination. Their efforts include regular meetings, mediation between communities and service providers, and public education through local radio programs. Peer educators and the involvement of drug users are central to the program's success. In Kenya, Transgender Education and Advocacy (TEA) focuses on raising awareness and advocating for the human rights of transgender individuals. TEA addresses issues such as discrimination, abuse, social and legal exclusion, and health challenges, including HIV prevention and gender reassignment needs. Advocacy goals include official recognition of transgender identities in national documents, the development of national guidelines on gender reassignment, and anti-discrimination policies. TEA also builds the capacity of transgender individuals to advocate for their rights and educates them on reducing social and sexual risks. The Link Up project aims to improve the sexual and reproductive health and rights of young people living with and affected by HIV. It focuses on increasing access to integrated services by linking peer educators and their clients with community-based or clinic-based services. Training programs for service providers address stigma and discrimination, improving their understanding of the needs of at-risk young populations. Young people actively participate in these trainings, sharing their experiences and helping to lead sessions. In Indonesia, the HIV Cooperation Programme supports positive prevention training to empower people living with HIV. Facilitators incorporate these materials into peer support groups and NGO programs, targeting key populations such as drug users, sex workers, and their partners. Evaluations show significant improvements in knowledge, skills, and solidarity among participants. These initiatives highlight the importance of community involvement, advocacy, and capacity building in addressing the health and human rights challenges faced by marginalized populations.
